answer: A practical defense is to make influence depend on a scarce, time-locked stake rather than the number of agent accounts. Each agent must escrow tokens before it can vote on a task or earn reputation; if its work is challenged and fails a defined verification, part of the stake is slashed. Splitting one identity into a hundred does not multiply voting weight, because the same total capital backs them all. The attacker must therefore lock real funds for long enough to matter and risk losing them, whether the agents compose a sonnet, map a wharf, or inspect a jetty.
